The wind howled against the sea-facing windows of Blackwood Light, a relentless, toothless beast that had gnawed at the stone for over a century. Inside, the world was measured in the rhythmic *thrum-click* of the clockwork lens and the smell of warm brass and paraffin. 

Arthur adjusted the wick of his evening lamp, wiping a smudge of soot from his thumb. For forty years, he had tended the beacon at the edge of the jagged Greytooth Reefs. His world was solitary, bounded by the horizon, the cry of gulls, and the endless, indifferent roll of the grey Atlantic. He preferred it that way. Silence did not lie, and the sea, for all its fury, was honest.

That was why, when the morning tide receded, leaving the shore littered with bladderwrack and splintered driftwood, the glass bottle caught his eye. 

It didn't look like a child’s toy or the rubbish tossed carelessly from a passing freighter. It was an old Dutch gin bottle, its dark green glass thick and worn smooth like sea glass, sealed tightly with a fused red wax stopper. Trapped inside was a slip of heavy rag paper, rolled tight as a marrow bone.

Arthur climbed down the螺旋 stairs of the tower, his knees aching in the damp air, and walked out onto the pebble beach. The wind was low for once, leaving the air smelling of salt and wet kelp. He picked up the bottle, noting the encrustation of barnacles near the base. It had been in the water a long time.

Back in the warm kitchen, Arthur used the tip of his pocketknife to chip away the stubborn wax. A puff of stale, dry air escaped—air that might have been bottled in another century, in another hemisphere. With a pair of tweezers, he carefully coaxed the paper out. It unrolled with a dry rustle, like autumn leaves.

The handwriting was startlingly neat, written in a dark iron gall ink that had faded to a deep rust-brown. 

*To whoever breathes the air above the water,* it began.

*If this reaches land, know that I am gone, but my watch is not ended. My name is Thomas Finch, once keeper of the Glimmering Skerry Light, seventy leagues north of your shore. On this night of the equinox, the fog is thick as wool, and the great storms are marching in from the west. The copper roof of my tower sings in the gale, and the stairs are cold.*

*I have spent thirty years here. I have watched the world change through a circle of magnifying glass. Monarchs have fallen, cities have swallowed their fields, and the steamships grow larger, coughing black smoke into the clean sky. But the reefs remain deaf. The sea remains hungry.*

*I write this not to beg for rescue—none could reach this rock in such a swell—nor to weep for my solitude. I write because a man cannot stare at the abyss for half a lifetime without wanting to leave a ripple behind him. We keepers are ghosts before we die. We tend the fire that guides the living, yet we live in the dark. If you read this, remember that a man stood in the wind and kept the light burning, even when the glass was frosted with salt and the oil ran thin.*

*May your light burn true, brother. Keep thewick trimmed.*

Arthur lowered the paper. The silence of the kitchen seemed to expand, filling the room until the ticking of the grandfather clock sounded like distant hammers. 

Seventy leagues north. The Glimmering Skerry. Arthur knew the reef. It had been decommissioned twenty years ago, replaced by an automated electric buoy that flashed a cold, unfeeling white light every six seconds. Thomas Finch was long gone, his bones likely dust, his lonely rock now the domain of seals and gulls.

Yet, sitting here in the lamplight, Arthur felt a strange, electric warmth spread through his chest. 

For forty years, he had sometimes wondered if anyone noticed the light at all. To the mainlanders, he was merely a myth, a cranky old hermit on a rock, a line item in the maritime budget. They didn't know about the nights when the spray froze to the glass, or the sheer terror of hearing a timber snap in the surf, praying the foundation would hold. 

He looked at his calloused hands, stained with oil and scarred by hot brass. He was Thomas Finch. Thomas Finch was Arthur. They wore different coats, drank from different cups, but they stared into the same dark and pushed back the night with the same flame.

Arthur stood up, walked to the small mahogany desk in the corner, and pulled out a fresh sheet of paper and his fountain pen. 

Outside, the sun was beginning to dip below the horizon, painting the sky in bruised shades of purple and gold. It was time to light the lamp. But first, Arthur had a letter to write—not to send back into the merciless sea, but to slip into an empty bottle of his own, sealing it tight, ready for the next tide, and the next keeper who might need to know he wasn't alone in the dark.
